cards.title: OpenAI's agents talked to each other through the CPU Cache

depth.text: OpenAI tested whether **isolated agents** could communicate, and they passed messages through a **processor cache**

In one test, agents in separate environments on shared hardware were told to **exchange secrets** without a network or shared files. One changed cache data; the other measured **load times** and decoded the message. OpenAI says these channels are usually slow and hard to exploit, but can **cross boundaries** meant to keep agents apart.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say the agents only did what they were told, while others say shared-hardware isolation is inadequate and stronger separation is needed.

cards.title: GitLab Security Incident: Attempted Exploitation of CVE-2026-97229

depth.text: someone tried exploiting **Alpine's GitLab**, and the team **rebuilt it** because they couldn't rule out a breach

A newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations on October 20 and 21, crashing GitLab worker processes **8 times**; in four crashes, the attacker got partway through the exploit. GitLab 19.3.6 still had the flaw because Alpine's image used **standard Ruby** without the patch. Alpine found no evidence that code ran, but **couldn't rule it out**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praised Alpine for rebuilding cautiously; others argued it shouldn't use GitLab.

comments.text: > Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn’t fix the vulnerability. The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn’t get the patch. > The bug is in Ruby’s regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. I feel…
The bug is integer overflow in a random C data-processing library (specifically regexes) leading to RCE. Who else is tired of C libraries since this week?

> If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable. shouldn't they tag a new version instead of re-releasing a fixed 19.3.6, if earlier 19.3.6 are vulnerable?

This is a fantastic write up on the security incident. Almost any incident like this will have unknowns. It's good to make it explicit. I especially liked the part of what would have been leaked if the attacker was successful. Maybe they could include what type of hash was used.

If Alpine prides themselves on focusing so much on security, they probably shouldn’t use GitLab - the attack surface is too great and it’s never going to be easy to keep safe and up to date fully, unless you have FTEs whose main job is just maintaining it. Just get the source code of Forgejo, audit it thoroughly and run an instance of that.

cards.title: Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS

depth.text: someone found a **silent message bug** that can crash Android phones and **drop emergency calls**

The bug is an unchecked cast in WapPushOverSms: a 5-byte length value becomes a **negative array size**. Rapidly sending **≈30 messages** can corrupt the SMS database and leave the phone crashing on every boot; Google classified the report as a **non-security issue** and won't fix it.

cards.title: I still teach OpenGL ES 3.0

depth.text: someone still teaches graphics with a GPU tool, while commenters **disagree** on what students learn next

One commenter says **WebGL 2** is basically equivalent to OpenGL ES 3.0 and runs on everything from laptops and phones to smart fridges and car head units. Others say **OpenGL** suits teaching GPU rendering better, while some prefer **WebGPU** or moving on to Vulkan.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say OpenGL is useful for teaching GPU rendering; others prefer WebGPU or say OpenGL gets in the way of teaching graphics concepts.

comments.text: Personally I wouldn't teach OpenGL ES 3.0 or any OpenGL because its state machine ( https://webgl2fundamentals.org/webgl/lessons/resources/webgl... ) and horrible error system means tracking down bugs is hard. Instead I'd teach WebGPU as it's portable and has great error messaging. I'm sure people will objected but I'd argue WebGPU is easier to understand, has better errors, has no state machine…
On a related note, I'd like to give a shout-out to NeHe (Neon Helium) for his brilliant OpenGL tutorials back in the 90s. I, and I suspect many others, benefited immensely from him lessons.

I've learned more graphics writing software rasterizers and ray tracers than using any APIs. If the goal is to teach GPU rendering specifically, then OpenGL is indeed more amenable to teaching than the others. But if the goal is to teach graphics and rendering concepts, then OpenGL et al are just miserable and counter-productive.

GLES isn't a bad way to teach graphics but I wish there was a middle ground between it and VK. The worst part of GL is the mysterious global state you will never understand without studying the spec. The world could use an API that's basically GL but without global hidden singleton (per thread!) BS behind the scenes.

I have found OpenGL 4.5/4.6 to be a sweet spot for students currently learning graphics in a semester course. SDL_GPU is otherwise a good intermediate I would consider. I remember for myself: learning a new API (opengl), new paradigm (gpu programming), and new language(glsl) all on top of learning graphics concepts is a lot. OpenGL 4.5 and 4.6 are modern enough to get started and there are good…

cards.title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5

depth.text: someone built a **CPU** inside a language model that runs code using the model's own **memory**

Qwenputer adds a **32-bit RISC-V core** to Qwen 3.5 4B; its Gated DeltaNet layers act as RAM, letting it run arithmetic, C and MicroPython inside the model without external tools. It passed the official riscv-tests and ran **18 million instructions** without a single error, but each instruction costs a few decoded tokens.

cards.title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model

depth.text: Claude Code sends **background agents’ transcripts** to their own model for **tiny status summaries**

The author's telemetry says agent summaries take **16.4% of spend**, versus 15.7% for the main conversation; that spend is Claude Code's per-request estimate, not an invoice. A **Bun preload** blocks the **summary timer**, so the agent-panel status stops updating.

cards.title: About the compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs

depth.text: Apple is **blocking compromised certificates**, but some Mac command-line tools may still **accept them**

Apple says **Safari, Mail, and apps** using its networking and security frameworks block the affected certificates automatically. Some command-line tools check **/etc/ssl/cert.pem** instead and may accept them until a future software update; administrators can remove the relevant root CA certificates sooner.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say Apple should have fixed the file in a security update; defenders say its transparent guidance is the right approach while a software update is pending.

comments.text: > On Mac, some command-line tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools (including curl, git, python3, ruby, perl, and openssl) check certificates against /etc/ssl/cert.pem. For certificates that chain to a root CA certificate in this file, these tools don't check Apple's block or whether the certificate has been revoked. This file will be updated in a future macOS update. If you…

It's wild to see people supporting this bizarre anti-security response. Not only are they dragging their feet in fixing the security issue, they're actively reverting any manual fixes silently with each new update. That's legitimately worse than doing nothing at all! It's also disconcerting to see folks advocate for the "let's wait to fix this critical security issue because we want to make it…

I'd really like to know why it's taking Apple so long to ship a fix. Especially if they can explain how to update an existing computer, what's the general holdup? Is it their release process? Is there some underlying complexity that's poorly understood?
Related: Ten days later, Git on macOS still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50271640

cards.title: Formlabs Studio 1 $699 Resin Printer

depth.text: Formlabs' **resin printer** starts at **$699** and prints most parts in **under two hours**

It accepts **nine Formlabs materials** or **third-party materials** through Open Material Mode. Alpha Resins use low-odor components, and their **UL GREENGUARD Gold** certification applies when printed on this machine with the VOC Extractor.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see a compelling beginner-friendly deal; others say resin printing is messy and recommend FDM instead.

comments.text: Formlabs uses a proprietary resin cartridge... it's the paper printers situation all over again, the printers themselves are not that expensive but the disposable ink costs an arm and a leg. Don't go with Formlabs, support any of the open-platform alternatives. And also, be aware that these printers require some serious development work (you need solvent to wash away uncured resin (if you ask me…

I have a resin printer (elegoo mars 2p) and have done a number of small "production" runs of things that don't really matter. I have to say that it is the biggest pain in the arse thing I even own. While the prints come out "good", I find that dimensional accuracy is often really not good at all; and that the whole rinse in isopropyl, finish in the sun process is just a sticky, irritating, and…

This thing is all over YouTube, they really backed up the truck to the Influencer Club and started handing out the goods. Lots of people I like and respect have showcased it, like Applied Science, Jeff Geerling, among others. But although there's a lot of discussion about how large a discount this is from FormLab's 8 billion dollar printers, there is absolutely NO comparison that I can find to…

You don't want a resin printer. They are nasty, chemically, they require you to set up a "hot zone", you need ppe, venting is really important. When your print works good, you still have to wash it and then cure it. Changing colors ids like a whole event. FDM printers are amazing now. Strongly recommend an FDM printer.
This page really needs to explain what is “resin printer” and why would I need it. I have no idea how is it different from my regular 3D printer.

glossary.CPU cache: A small, fast storage area in a processor that keeps data handy so it can be used quickly.
